content: 1. The initial diagnostic test for pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) in individuals who screen positive for TB should include a chest X-ray to support further investigations. For extrapulmonary TB, additional investigations should be conducted as applicable. 2. The lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay (LF-LAM) is recommended to assist in TB diagnosis among individuals with symptoms and signs of TB, particularly those with CD4 counts ≤200 cells/mm³ (inpatients) or ≤100 cells/mm³ (outpatients). It is also applicable for any CD4 count in symptomatic or seriously ill individuals. 3. Cryptococcal antigen screening is recommended for individuals with CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³ and should be considered for those with CD4 counts ≤200 cells/mm³. 4. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for individuals with CD4 counts <350 cells/mm³ or those in clinical stages 3 or 4 of HIV. It is also recommended for any CD4 count in settings with high prevalence of malaria or severe bacterial infections. 5. TB preventive treatment should be provided in accordance with current WHO guidelines. 6. Fluconazole pre-emptive therapy is recommended for individuals who test positive for cryptococcal antigen but do not have evidence of meningitis, particularly those with CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³. 7. Rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation is recommended for individuals with advanced HIV disease, except in cases where clinical symptoms suggest meningitis (TB or cryptococcal). In such cases, ART initiation should be deferred. 8. Tailored adherence support, including counseling and home visits if feasible, is recommended for individuals with CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³ to ensure optimal adherence to the advanced HIV disease package. 9. Cryptococcal disease is a significant opportunistic infection among individuals with advanced HIV disease and a major contributor to mortality. Cryptococcus neoformans, the causative agent, is acquired through inhalation and is present in the environment worldwide. 10. Early diagnosis and treatment of cryptococcal meningitis are critical to reducing mortality. Healthcare professionals should maintain a low threshold for suspecting cryptococcal meningitis in individuals with advanced HIV disease. 11. Countries should prioritize access to rapid diagnostic cryptococcal antigen assays, preferably lateral flow assays, for use in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), serum, plasma, or whole blood. 12. Immediate ART initiation is not recommended for individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to the risk of increased mortality. ART should be deferred for 4–6 weeks after initiating antifungal treatment. 13. For diagnosing cryptococcal meningitis, a lumbar puncture with CSF opening pressure measurement and rapid cryptococcal antigen assay is the preferred approach in settings with access to these tests and rapid results. 14. In settings without access to rapid cryptococcal antigen assays, a lumbar puncture with CSF India ink examination is recommended. 15. In cases where lumbar puncture is contraindicated, rapid serum, plasma, or whole-blood cryptococcal antigen assays are the preferred diagnostic approaches. 16. Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy is recommended for individuals with CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³ to prevent invasive cryptococcal disease before initiating or reinitiating ART. 17. Fluconazole primary prophylaxis is recommended for individuals with CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³ in settings where cryptococcal antigen screening is unavailable. 18. The preferred induction treatment for cryptococcal meningitis includes amphotericin B deoxycholate and flucytosine. Alternative regimens include fluconazole combined with flucytosine or amphotericin B combined with fluconazole. 19. For the consolidation phase, fluconazole is recommended for eight weeks following the induction phase. 20. Maintenance therapy (secondary prophylaxis) with fluconazole is recommended to prevent relapse of cryptococcal meningitis. 21. Routine use of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy during the induction phase of cryptococcal meningitis treatment is not recommended. 22. Raised intracranial pressure, a common feature of cryptococcal meningitis, should be managed with therapeutic lumbar punctures to relieve pressure. Repeat lumbar punctures may be necessary until symptoms resolve or CSF pressure normalizes. 23. Clinical response to treatment should be assessed daily during the initial two weeks of induction therapy. Routine follow-up lumbar punctures after completing induction therapy are not recommended in lowand middle-income countries. 24. For individuals with cryptococcal meningitis relapse, induction treatment should be restarted, raised intracranial pressure managed, and adherence support provided. ART initiation should be deferred for 4–6 weeks after optimal antifungal therapy. 25. Paradoxical cryptococcal immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) occurs in 10–50% of individuals with cryptococcal disease initiating ART and is associated with high mortality. Raised intracranial pressure is a common feature of IRIS and contributes to mortality. 26. Disseminated histoplasmosis, caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, is a frequent clinical presentation among individuals with HIV. Symptoms are nonspecific and may mimic other infectious diseases, complicating diagnosis and treatment. 27. Diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis in individuals with HIV should be based on detecting circulating Histoplasma antigens. Amphotericin B is recommended for initial treatment, followed by itraconazole for maintenance therapy.
